title: All-vs-Nothing Operational Manifestation of Preparation Contextuality
authors: Jayashree Karmakar, Rafiuddin Gazi, Biswadeep Chatterjee, Subhendu B Ghosh, Anandamay Das Bhowmik, Ananya Chakraborty, Manik Banik
abstract: Preparation contextuality is often manifested operationally through a quantitative advantage over preparation-noncontextual models in information-processing tasks, yet quantum theory typically falls short of perfect success. Here we introduce a parity-oblivious Hidden Matching task that instead yields an all-vs-nothing manifestation of preparation contextuality. Alice encodes an $n$-bit string so that her message reveals no information about any input parity other than the two-bit parities. Bob, given a perfect matching on the input positions, must output an edge of the matching together with the parity of its two bits. A quantum protocol using a single $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$-qubit message satisfies the parity-obliviousness constraint and succeeds with certainty. We prove that no preparation-noncontextual model achieves perfect success for any even $n\ge6$. The result holds for arbitrary ontic state spaces and assumes neither outcome determinism nor measurement noncontextuality. For $n=6$ and $n=8$, the optimal noncontextual success probabilities are $4/5$ and $3/4$, respectively, while asymptotically the optimal noncontextual success probability is $1/2+Θ(1/\sqrt n)$. Our asymptotic upper bound follows from a Fourier-analytic sum rule derived via hypercontractivity on the Boolean hypercube. The resulting separation is qualitative rather than merely quantitative: quantum theory achieves perfect success, whereas preparation-noncontextual models cannot. We aslo show that at $n=8$ the noncontextual bound remains $3/4$ even when Bob is restricted to just suitable $4$ of the $105$ possible perfect matchings, bringing the effect within experimental reach.
summary: This paper introduces the parity-oblivious Hidden Matching task to demonstrate an 'all-vs-nothing' test for preparation contextuality. It shows that quantum mechanics achieves perfect success in this task, whereas any model assuming preparation noncontextuality fails to achieve perfect success for $n \ge 6$. The work establishes a fundamental, qualitative distinction between quantum theory and classical assumptions about preparation.
main_problem: To demonstrate an 'all-vs-nothing' operational manifestation of preparation contextuality, moving beyond previous quantitative advantages.
main_result: Quantum theory achieves perfect success in the parity-oblivious Hidden Matching task, while no preparation-noncontextual model can achieve perfect success for even $n \ge 6$.
method: The impossibility proof involves reducing the problem to a finite-dimensional convex optimization problem over Fourier polynomials, utilizing hypercontractivity and Fourier-analytic sum rules.
model_or_system: The task is the parity-oblivious Hidden Matching (PoHMn), where Alice encodes an $n$-bit string, and Bob must identify an edge and its parity from a perfect matching $M$. The framework relies on comparing operational quantum predictions against those derived from ontological models assuming preparation noncontextuality.
key_observables: The success probability of the task, specifically the perfect success rate for quantum vs. the upper bound for noncontextual models.
important_parameters: The size of the input string $n$, and the specific case values $n=6$ and $n=8$ where the noncontextual bounds are $4/5$ and $3/4$, respectively.
main_assumptions: The result holds for arbitrary ontic state spaces and assumes neither outcome determinism nor measurement noncontextuality.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the PoHMn task setup for $n=6$ and show how the quantum protocol achieves certainty while the noncontextual model fails to do so.
paper_structure: The paper first reviews the ontological model framework for operational theories, then defines the PoHMn task, establishes the impossibility proof for noncontextual models, and finally presents the quantum protocol and quantitative bounds.
why_interesting: It provides a strong, qualitative separation between quantum mechanics and classical assumptions (preparation noncontextuality) using a structured information-theoretic task, which is a key area of modern quantum foundations.

Alice holds an n-bit string x and sends Bob a single message, subject to the constraint that it reveal nothing about any parity xS with |S| ̸= 0, 2; the two-bit parities xi ⊕xj are exempt. Bob holds one of the (n −1)!! perfect matchings of [n], here M ≡{{1, 4}, {2, 3}, {5, 6}} ∈M6, and must return one of its edges together with the parity of the two bits it joins. Which edge he answers about is his choice, and Alice does not learn the matching.

FIG. 2. (Color online) The antipodal matching, illustrated for n = 12. (a) The elements of [n] are placed around a circle so that each part of P ≡P1 ⊔P2 ⊔P3 occupies a consecutive arc (here |P1| = 5, |P2| = 4, |P3| = 3, all at most n/2). The dashed diameters are the edges {vp, vp+n/2} of M; none has both endpoints in one part. (b) If a part spans more than n/2 positions, it contains an antipodal pair (red), since any arc through both p and p+n/2 has at least n/2+1 positions.
